Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

Airbnb (ABNB) stock returned 53.2% over the past twelve months, against 11.0% for the S&P 500. After that rise, the question is what could lift the shares next. Airbnb is already large, taking nearly 0.5 million bookings a day. During its November 5, 2026 call, management named one business growing faster than its core business. What is that business, and how far along is Airbnb with it?

All of that 53.2% came from the share price, because Airbnb pays no dividend. Part of your money can pay you income while you wait for the next move. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics.

Airbnb Now Lists Thousands Of Hotels

The business is hotels. The platform now lists thousands of boutique and independent hotels across more than 60 top destinations. During the November 5 call, management said hotel bookings accelerated again in the third quarter of fiscal 2026. Hotels are also growing markedly faster than Airbnb's core business.

It is still early, though. Hotels are growing "off of a very, very tiny base," in management's words. Management said the hotel industry has also come round to Airbnb, after some animosity in the early 2010s. In its view, hotels now see it as a major ally, because it brings them an audience that is disproportionately Gen Z.

How Big Could Hotels Get For Airbnb?

Management called hotels a $900 billion market. It said Airbnb will make multiple billions of dollars in hotel revenue in the coming years.

To view that against the whole company, Airbnb recorded revenue of $13.9 billion over the twelve months to September 30, 2026. That was up 16.7%, following growth of 10.2% in the twelve months before. A few billion dollars from hotels would be a large addition to Airbnb, not a sideline.

Airbnb stock trades at 7.6 times sales, against 3.1 for the S&P 500. On November 18, the shares closed 5.4% below their highest close of the past year. Buyers at that price appear to assume the company keeps growing well ahead of the market, and hotels offer one place that growth could come from.

What Does Airbnb Still Have To Prove?

Airbnb still has to give a forecast for hotels. On the November 5 call, management declined to give any projection for the hotel business. Until it does, you cannot measure how much hotels add.

New businesses also cost money, and that shows in how much of each booking Airbnb keeps. The share of bookings Airbnb kept as revenue was 17.6% in the third quarter, down slightly from a year earlier. Management said that was mainly due to Reserve Now, Pay Later, which lets guests book now and pay closer to the stay. A smaller part came from incentives and credits for new business initiatives.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Booking Holdings (BKNG) expects its room nights to grow 1% to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2026. Management gave that guidance on its November 3, 2026 call. Room nights are the nights travelers book through its sites. They offer the plainest count of the travel Booking sells. The guidance would mark a clear slowdown from the third quarter. So why is Booking expecting room-night growth to slow?

Why Booking Holdings Expects Slower Room-Night Growth

Management gave two reasons for the slower growth. Booking faces its toughest year-earlier comparison of 2026. It is also unsure how recent events will affect travel demand. In October, demand was hit by disrupted travel to and from the Middle East, elevated airfares and localized unrest in certain European cities. Management's guide assumes the effects of the Middle East conflict last through the end of the year.

Room nights grew 7% in the third quarter, accelerating from 5% in the second quarter and topping management's own guidance.

Booking also expects slower sales growth and flat profit. Management expects adjusted revenue, the company's own measure, to grow 0% to 2% in the fourth quarter, after rising 9% in the third. It expects adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure, to be about flat from a year earlier. Part of the reason is that it plans to spend more on flights, attractions, dining and AI.

Will Booking Holdings' Slowdown Last Into 2027?

Management has not said yet. The company plans to discuss 2027 in February with its fourth-quarter results. Executives did offer early signs on both sides.

On the hopeful side, management said its on-the-book statistics for the first half of 2027 look healthy. It called them a very early indicator, still subject to cancellations. Booking's alternative accommodation listings grew 9% in the third quarter. Management called that an encouraging signal for future growth in that category.

On the other side, management said travel demand was resilient in the third quarter but moderated somewhat toward its end. How long the slowdown lasts remains an open question for holders.

How Hard Has Booking Holdings Stock Been Hit?

Booking Holdings stock has lost 22.8% over the past year, against a 10.3% gain for the S&P 500. The shares trade at 16.1 times earnings, against 22.0 for the S&P 500. At the end of September, before the outlook, Booking's P/E was already the second lowest of 40 quarter ends since December 2016. Today's 16.1 is lower still, so the price likely assumes slower growth ahead.

title: Airbnb vs. Shopify: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Will the future of growth be driven by global travel experiences or the expansion of independent digital commerce? Deciding between Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)and Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP)involves choosing between two very different platform leaders.

Airbnb connects millions of travelers with unique stays, while Shopify provides the software backbone for modern retail. Both companies benefit from powerful network effects, where more users or merchants make the platform more valuable for everyone involved.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates as a massive marketplace for lodging and experiences, connecting more than 5 million hosts with guests in roughly 220 countries. In its latest annual report, the company highlights its reliance on Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) for platform hosting and its use of third-party providers for community support. As the platform evolves, it is exploring the use of AI in travel to enhance its search capabilities and host support.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $13.9 billion. This represents a revenue growth of approximately 16.7% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During the same time frame, the company reported net income of nearly $3.2 billion.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with liquid assets, reached roughly 1.4x. The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0.3x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $4.6 billion, though note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.

The case for Shopify

Shopify serves as the central operating system for millions of merchants across 175 countries, providing tools for both online and in-store sales. The company supports everyone from small entrepreneurs to large enterprise brands, relying on partners like PayPal and Stripe for payment processing. This ecosystem approach allows it to scale without owning inventory, creating a software-centric business model with high recurring potential.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $14.2 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of roughly 32.5% over the preceding period. Shopify also reported a net income of approximately $2.1 billion for these twelve months.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 6.0x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.0x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $2.0 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation.
